introduction: This guide is a hundred counsels: short commands and longer advice from Bahá’u’lláh, the Báb and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá on how to live. Be generous and thankful, truthful and trustworthy; do not backbite or look for faults; let deeds match words; teach with wisdom; hold firm; use the time. Many are addressed to one person by name. Beside them stand a hundred counsels from elsewhere: the commandments and the Proverbs, the Sermon on the Mount and the letters of Paul and James, Luqman's advice to his son in the Qur’an, the Sayings of the Fathers, Confucius, the Dhammapada, Marcus Aurelius and Aristotle. A few voices, Shakespeare's Portia and Polonius, Paul against himself, Thoreau, Machiavelli and the Preacher, ask why good advice is so much easier to give than to follow.
questions: Choose one counsel from the guide that you find hard. What makes it hard, and does any outside voice help?
"Whatever a man's tongue speaketh, that let him prove by his deeds." Portia and Paul both admit how far knowing is from doing. What closes the gap?
Several counsels forbid fault-finding and backbiting, as do the Qur’an, James and the Dhammapada. Why is this given such weight in the life of a community?
Polonius says, "to thine own self be true"; these counsels begin from the fear of God. Do the two lead to the same honesty?
Teaching is to be done "with wisdom." What do Jesus's "wise as serpents," Paul's "seasoned with salt" and the Qur’an's "fair exhortation" suggest that means in practice?
Rabbi Tarfon said the work is not yours to finish, yet you may not desist. How does that sit with the urgency of the last passages?

outside.why: The Qur’an praises those who spend in ease and in adversity, who control their wrath and are forgiving toward others.
Muḥammad said that no one has faith until he wishes for his brother what he wishes for himself.
Jesus sums up the law and the prophets in the same rule: do to others what you would have them do to you.
Luqman counsels his son in the Qur’an not to turn his cheek in scorn toward people nor walk the earth with pertness.
This is the verse of the Qur’an that the passage echoes: work not confusion in the earth after its fair ordering.
A psalm asks who may dwell on God's holy hill, and answers: the one who speaks the truth in his heart and does no evil to his neighbour.
Micah sums up what is required: to do justly, to love mercy and to walk humbly with God.
Thoreau said that if he knew a man was coming to his house with the conscious design of doing him good, he would run for his life. What keeps kindness and service from becoming what he feared?
Marcus Aurelius tells himself to stop talking about what a good man ought to be, and be one.
Shakespeare's Portia says that she could easier teach twenty what were good to be done than be one of the twenty to follow her own teaching. Why are counsels easier to give than to keep?
The letter of James asks for doers of the word, and not hearers only.
Paul confesses that the good he would do he does not, and the evil he would not, that he does. "Blessed are they who act." What stands between hearing a counsel and acting on it?
Jesus says that a tree is known by its fruit, and people by what they bring forth.
Jesus says: let your light so shine that others may see your good works.
Aristotle held that we become just by doing just acts, and brave by doing brave ones.
A sage of the Mishnah advises judging every person with the scale weighted in his favour.
Jesus asks why we see the speck in a brother's eye and not the beam in our own.
The Dhammapada says that a sage should take notice of his own misdeeds and not of the failings of others.
The Qur’an forbids suspicion, spying and backbiting, and likens backbiting to eating a brother's flesh.
The letter of James says: speak not evil one of another; who art thou that judgest another?
The Qur’an says that the servants of the Merciful walk modestly, and when the foolish address them they answer: peace.
Confucius says that when we see men of worth we should think of equalling them, and when we see the contrary we should examine ourselves.
Shakespeare's Polonius grounds honesty in being true to oneself. These counsels ground it in the fear of God. Which root holds better?
Jesus asks for speech so plain that yes means yes and no means no.
Jesus says that whoever is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much.
Machiavelli advised that a prudent ruler should not keep faith when it turns against him. What becomes of a society in which trustworthiness is treated as a policy?
Proverbs says that a man diligent in his business shall stand before kings.
The Qur’an says that God enjoins justice and kindness and forbids lewdness, abomination and wickedness.
The Preacher concludes: fear God and keep his commandments, for this is the whole duty of man.
The second table of the commandments forbids killing, adultery, theft, false witness and coveting.
Gamaliel gave the same advice to a council: let them alone, lest you be found fighting against God.
The letter of James says that the wisdom from above is pure, peaceable, gentle and without partiality.
Jesus calls the peacemakers blessed, for they shall be called the children of God.
The letter of James points to the patience of Job and the end that was given him.
Paul says: as much as lies in you, live peaceably with all.
Paul asks his readers to think on whatever is true, honest, just, pure and lovely.
Kant called enlightenment the courage to use one's own understanding, and release from tutelage.
The Qur’an says that whoever believes in God has grasped a firm handhold that will never break.
Jesus calls blessed the pure in heart, for they shall see God.
Deuteronomy asks what the Lord requires: to fear him, walk in his ways, love him and serve him, for thy good.
The Preacher says: whatever thy hand finds to do, do it with thy might.
Paul says to do every task heartily, as to the Lord and not to men.
Paul tells Timothy to be an example in word, in conduct, in love and in faith.
Isaiah says that all the goodliness of flesh is as the flower of the field, which fades.
The Dhammapada sums up the teaching: not to do evil, to do good and to purify one's mind.
Paul says: let us not be weary in well doing, for in due season we shall reap.
Proverbs praises a woman clothed with strength and honour, on whose tongue is the law of kindness.
Jesus tells his followers that they are the light of the world, a city set on a hill.
The first psalm likens the faithful to a tree planted by rivers of water.
Jesus says to seek first the kingdom of God, and that the rest will be added.
Jesus sends his disciples out as sheep among wolves and asks them to be wise as serpents and harmless as doves.
The Qur’an says: call to the way of thy Lord with wisdom and fair exhortation.
Peter asks believers to be ready to give a reason for their hope, with meekness.
Paul asks that speech be always with grace, seasoned with salt, so as to answer each person rightly.
Jesus asks what it profits a man to gain the whole world and lose his own soul.
Proverbs says that purposes fail without counsel, and are established by many counsellors.
The Qur’an tells the Prophet to consult with his companions in the conduct of affairs.
The Qur’an speaks of the one who takes his own desire for his god.
Isaiah hears that the fast God has chosen is to loose the bands of wickedness and share bread with the hungry. How does keeping a fast from sunrise to sunset relate to that?
Jesus tells those who fast to do it without show, before the Father who sees in secret.
Paul asks that each bear the burdens of the other, and so fulfil the law of Christ.
Paul says that he has learned to be content in whatever state he is.
The letter to the Hebrews asks its readers to hold fast without wavering.
This is the story of the calf in Exodus, to which the passage refers.
Moses says: I have set before you life and death; therefore choose life.
The letter of James says: draw near to God, and he will draw near to you.
The first letter of John says: love not the world, for the world passes away.
FitzGerald's Omar asks only for a loaf, a jug of wine and a companion beneath the bough. What does a counsel against being beguiled by the world say to someone who finds the world enough?
Jesus says that the gate is narrow and the way hard that leads to life.
The Preacher advises: be not righteous over much. Is there such a thing as too much observance, and what would these counsels say?
Paul says that tribulation works patience, and patience experience, and experience hope.
Paul asks the Thessalonians to pray without ceasing and give thanks in everything.
A psalm says: fret not thyself because of evildoers, for they shall soon be cut down like the grass.
A psalm calls God a refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.
Isaiah promises perfect peace to the one whose mind is stayed on God.
The letter of Jude praises the one who is able to keep us from falling.
Paul asks the Corinthians to be steadfast and unmoveable, knowing that their labour is not in vain.
Isaiah hears: fear thou not, for I am with thee; be not dismayed.
Jesus called fishermen from their nets and said he would make them fishers of men.
The Qur’an says: hold fast, all together, to the cable of God, and do not separate.
Paul lists his own labours and journeys, in weariness and watchings often.
Jesus says: I must work while it is day; the night comes, when no one can work.
Jesus tells his disciples to proclaim on the housetops what they have heard in the ear.
A psalm says: I love the Lord, because he has heard my voice.
Paul says that it is high time to awake, for the night is far spent.
Longfellow's psalm of life ends: let us, then, be up and doing, with a heart for any fate.
Rabbi Tarfon said that the day is short, the work plentiful, and the master of the house insistent.
Rabbi Tarfon added that it is not your duty to finish the work, but neither are you free to desist from it. How does that temper "work unceasingly"?
Proverbs says that a good name is to be chosen above great riches.
Shakespeare's Antony says that the evil men do lives after them, and the good is often buried with their bones. What kind of remembrance is promised here?
Proverbs says that the memory of the just is blessed, and the name of the wicked shall rot.
The Qur’an swears by the declining day that man is in loss, save those who believe, do good and exhort one another.
Paul asks his readers to walk carefully, as wise and not as fools, redeeming the time.
A psalm prays: teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts to wisdom.
Jesus says to labour for the food that endures to everlasting life.
Jesus says to leave the gift at the altar and first be reconciled with one's brother.
Paul says to put away bitterness, wrath and malice, and be kind to one another.
The Revelation of John ends with an invitation: let whoever is thirsty come and take the water of life freely.
Shelley's king left a boast on a ruin. What is it, according to this passage, that endures from a life?
The Qur’an tells believers to remember God with much remembrance and glorify him morning and evening.

james-speak-not-evil.text: Speak not evil one of another, brethren. He that speaketh evil of his brother, and judgeth his brother, speaketh evil of the law, and judgeth the law: but if thou judge the law, thou art not a doer of the law, but a judge

psalm-who-shall-abide.text: Lord, who shall abide in thy tabernacle? who shall dwell in thy holy hill? He that walketh uprightly, and worketh righteousness, and speaketh the truth in his heart. He that backbiteth not with his tongue, nor doeth evil to his neighbour, nor taketh up a reproach against his neighbour

psalm-keep-thy-tongue-from-evil.text: Keep thy tongue from evil, and thy lips from speaking guile. Depart from evil, and do good; seek peace, and pursue it

proverbs-false-balance.text: A false balance is abomination to the Lord: but a just weight is his delight

matthew-yea-yea-nay-nay.text: But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil

ephesians-speak-every-man-truth.text: Wherefore putting away lying, speak every man truth with his neighbour: for we are members one of another

exodus-thou-shalt-not.text: Thou shalt not kill. Thou shalt not commit adultery. Thou shalt not steal. Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour. Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's

deuteronomy-what-doth-the-lord-require.text: And now, Israel, what doth the Lord thy God require of thee, but to fear the Lord thy God, to walk in all his ways, and to love him, and to serve the Lord thy God with all thy heart and with all thy soul

hebrews-provoke-unto-love.text: And let us consider one another to provoke unto love and to good works

isaiah-is-not-this-the-fast.text: Is not this the fast that I have chosen? to loose the bands of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens, and to let the oppressed go free, and that ye break every yoke? Is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry, and that thou bring the poor that are cast out to thy house? when thou seest the naked, that thou cover him; and that thou hide not thyself from thine own flesh

matthew-when-thou-fastest.text: Moreover when ye fast, be not, as the hypocrites, of a sad countenance: for they disfigure their faces, that they may appear unto men to fast. Verily I say unto you, They have their reward. But thou, when thou fastest, anoint thine head, and wash thy face; That thou appear not unto men to fast, but unto thy Father which is in secret: and thy Father, which seeth in secret, shall reward thee openly

matthew-fishers-of-men.text: And he saith unto them, Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men

proverbs-memory-of-the-just.text: The memory of the just is blessed: but the name of the wicked shall rot

proverbs-good-name.text: A good name is rather to be chosen than great riches, and loving favour rather than silver and gold

psalm-testimonies-before-kings.text: I will speak of thy testimonies also before kings, and will not be ashamed

ecclesiastes-righteous-over-much.text: Be not righteous over much; neither make thyself over wise: why shouldest thou destroy thyself

quran-turn-not-thy-cheek-in-scorn.text: Turn not thy cheek in scorn toward folk, nor walk with pertness in the land. Lo! Allah loveth not each braggart boaster.

quran-neither-backbite.text: O ye who believe! Shun much suspicion; for lo! some suspicion is a crime. And spy not, neither backbite one another. Would one of you love to eat the flesh of his dead brother? Ye abhor that (so abhor the other)! And keep your duty (to Allah). Lo! Allah is Relenting, Merciful.

quran-work-not-confusion.text: Work not confusion in the earth after the fair ordering (thereof). and call on Him in fear and hope. Lo! the mercy of Allah is nigh unto the good.

matthew-they-say-and-do-not.text: The scribes and the Pharisees sit in Moses' seat: All therefore whatsoever they bid you observe, that observe and do; but do not ye after their works: for they say, and do not

analects-men-of-worth.text: When we see men of worth, we should think of equaling them; when we see men of a contrary character, we should turn inwards and examine ourselves
analects-men-of-worth.author: Confucius

dhammapada-teaching-of-the-buddhas.text: Not to commit any sin, to do good, and to purify one's mind, that is the teaching of (all) the Awakened

dhammapada-not-the-perversities-of-other.text: Not the perversities of others, not their sins of commission or omission, but his own misdeeds and negligences should a sage take notice of

aristotle-just-by-doing-just-acts.text: we become just by doing just acts, temperate by doing temperate acts, brave by doing brave acts
aristotle-just-by-doing-just-acts.author: Aristotle

shakespeare-to-thine-own-self.text: to thine ownself be true, / And it must follow, as the night the day, / Thou canst not then be false to any man
shakespeare-to-thine-own-self.author: William Shakespeare
